- 3/2/25
- So many new little bits and pieces of information will find their way into your mind that you will never really have much use for until that situation comes up again, making you think that you have forgotten the information
- For example, I went on a little stint of watching painting restorations, and now have a semi-familiarity with the techniques used. I know polyurethane is disgusting slop shit that should never be used to cover paintings, and how ubiquitous hot tables are, and that rabbitskin glue is not great but is at least straightforward to get off of old canvas and that when using canvas linings you should fray the edges so the sharp edge isn’t telegraphed to the front, etc etc
- I don’t really have a use for any of this information (although, I’m sure, bits and bobs of it will occasionally float to serve me in some isolated instances of my life)
- But as cool as the phenomenon is of “you’ll likely find use for the information in the unlikeliest of places” is, I’m interested right now in the opposite; where and how the information lives in your head when you aren’t using it
- That information I listed previously is completely vacant from my mind for the vast majority of the time. It’s not like the fact is sitting in the corner of my thought processes, but I just don’t notice it until I look at it directly (like how you always see your nose but don’t notice it most of the time)
- No - the information is literally gonezo caput, completely out of my head
- I guess (?) this is where I, for the first time in a timespan of years, begin to relate the mind back to the brain, as until now I have taken pretty good care to refer only to my “mind” when talking about mental processes and have not really touched the brain
- but I feel the physical brain is relevant here again. Because, I assume, this information about polyurethane is stored in the brain, but my mind never really uses that part of the brain. Which is why you can recall such a vast field of information and experiences that you remember, but they are very much NOT all “active” at once
- Brain wise, the information is always stored somewhere to be retrieved
- But mind-experience wise, the information poofs the fuck out of your head, and suddenly floats back into your thought process at apt and convenient times when the subject comes up
- As though your brain is really good (or does its best) at knowing when your mind would “want” some field of stored information, and silently floats the relevant memories to your mind, which your mind graciously but unconciously picks up, and takes for granted how and why that piece of information conveniently resurfaced when it wanted it to even though it remained completely absent for all the time that it WASN’T wanted
- Which I suppose brings me to something I was talking about with someone recently, about how forgetting realizations doesn’t mean you no longer have them
- Tangentially related, I suppose
- For example, in a generic sense, you go through some novel thought process and arrive at a new realization you have not had before, and you can tell its profundity or importance and weight, it marking “a step forward”, etc
- And then you forget the bitch
- “What was that thing i realized again? Oh, I… fuck I don’t actually remember”
- It’s frustrating! Because you have LOST that new information you just got!
- Except no you haven’t. That’s the beauty of it
- It’s easy to look at the thing you realized, and see that as the brand new cutting edge of your own thought processes, and if you forget it, to feel like you have taken a step back, reverted, undone progress, and “at best” you will have to re-realize it at some point and “at worst” you will never get it back
- Untrue. The only reason your mind was able to follow that thought process and make that realization was because it was already in a place that facilitated that realization
- Or, in other words; the thought you had is not the cutting edge of your mind. The “cutting edge” IS the state that your mind is in, and that thought process was borne from that. Indeed, the realization is not your first step forward - it is your conscious mind “catching up” to what your unconscious mind already figured out. A chair in a pitch black room is still there when the light is off, and shining a light on it doesn’t mean that the chair only exists when the light is on it
- As such, the same essence of your mind that enabled the realization of the thing is also what’s going to enable behaviors that correspond to that realization. The explicit, in-your-face moment of realization is not what enables those behaviors, it is the underlying unconscious-mind state of mind that bubbles up BOTH the explicit realization AND, separately, the behaviors that go along with it
- Indeed, if you pay attention after a realization like that, far more often than not you’ll see that you’ve actually already recently been acting in accordance with the realization without even knowing, and before you actually realized it!
- Forgetting a realization consciously does not mean it is eradicated from your mind, it just means that you no longer know you know it, but don’t worry, you still know it

- Not worried abt that anymore

- As promised, I am coming back to this later. I don’t think there’s much of a NEED to expand on this, since in forcing conciseness I actually captured it pretty well, but here I go anyway
- This is actually a feeling from like 3 years ago that I only just remembered ever even having
- Essentially, I started making a lot of tangible progress abt three years ago, and a worry surfaced. In its most narcissistic form; will new people I meet not know how I great I am because they don’t know how not-great I used to be?
- Or, if I meet someone now, will they take for granted all my attributes and characteristics that I have worked so hard on, because they will not know where I came from?
- Essentially, it was an identity based worry, lodged into the framework of assumptions that people will only able to appreciate me the way I can appreciate me; if they knew every single little detail about me, and that if they knew every hardship I faced and all my lows, as a corollary, they would see how hard I fought and struggled to climb anyway, and as a result, how strong and impactful I really was
- After all, at the time, I was nowhere near perfect, and of course internally I knew that - but it felt like my greatest peak, and couldn’t reconcile the fact in my head that if someone saw me for the first time right then, they wouldn’t see someone standing at their peak, and instead would just see some person standing on a not-even-so-tall hill
- I don’t have the full picture in my head right now of where I went after that, but in essence, I stopped worrying about it for several reasons.
- one being I realized that my past, while a part of me, is nevertheless an entirely separate thing from who I am right now in this moment, and someone knowing my past actually has no impact on what I am now
- People don’t interact with ALL of you at once - they don’t approach you as a huge bucket containing your 25 year old self and your 17 year old self and your 12 year old self and your 5 year old self etc etc. Even if they KNOW all those things, they still can really only interact with you as you are right now in the present moment, because right now in the present moment, that’s all you are. You may remember all that other stuff, but it’s not happening right now. Keep moving
- Another reason I think I stopped worrying about that is… well I guess pretty tightly entwined with the reason I just gave, to the point of just being a rephrasing of it. You don’t need all that information to fully appreciate someone in front of you. In superficial terms - someone can fully admire the curve of your cheekbones without needing to know what they looked like 10 years ago. The “value” of your cheekbones is not predicated on what they looked like before, the “value” of your cheekbones comes entirely from how they look in the present, and how the person looking at them feels like in the present.
- Sure, the past can influence what they look like, and knowledge of what they looked like in the past may change how a person feels about them now looking at them, but that’s not because the past is “here” - they still just feel however they feel NOW, in the present
- I will come back to this in a while once I know how to phrase this all better, especially since it is so wide a topic and hits so many redundant areas I have already talked about that I’m having trouble finding wording that isn’t just me reexplaining something I have already come to well worn terms with a while ago

- Your own appearance is one of the most stable things you have in your life, and that shit ain’t stable at all!
- So fascinating our relationship with stability and change
- WHY are we so drawn to resisting change and keeping things as they are. Why is this something we must overcome
- Because there’s no REASON for use to prefer the way things were first as opposed to anything else besides the fact that the original way was first
- First doesn’t mean shit? As far as the quality of experiences go, the order in which experiences happen does not impact the quality of each one, except in how the remembrance of earlier ones affect later ones
- But it seems so many people become fixated on keeping things as they are, or as they were - there’s this sense of safety I suppose that comes from things being the same, and we want that sense of stability even if it comes at a massive detriment to many other aspects
- By which I guess this a big way to say that NOTHING is stable, and the only reason to really want stability and want to resist change is in the desire to experience the same thing over and over simply from the satisfaction and safety in knowing what the experience will be
- I think the more you allow yourself to enjoy learning, the less you want things to stay as they have been - learning is fundamentally, I suppose, just a love of new experiences built upon past experiences, which is exactly what everyone’s life is as they live it
- Once you accustom yourself to that, your entire life becomes a beautiful little everchanging garden
- Cutesy phrasing, of course, but true nonetheless - the only reward waiting for you by keeping things the same is nothing new

- Which caused a breakthrough in being able to phrase this following though
- “Oh, [me], that’s such nebulous reasoning! Something isn’t the case just because you FEEL like it isn’t the case, look at the FACTS!”
- Well. The facts are arbitrarily built upon a bunch of other people’s feelings. And I am listening to my own feelings. And my feelings tell me I didn’t make that shit. So I didn’t
- That IS the actual reason. Any logical reasoning is redundant and irrelevant because it’s not a logical topic - hardly anything is. It’s an emotional and personal and intimate topic, so I will trust my emotional and intimate self to tell me the answer
- I don’t feel it because I know it, I know it because I feel it, and I feel it because it’s true, and it’s true because I feel it
- “oh but but! That makes no sense! How can two separate things arise only when the other exists??”
- Well. can be answered one of two ways
- One: that contradiction only exists when you reduce the actual situation down to words. When you deal with defined categories, they have conflicts with each other, and you miss that the original things themselves are NOT the defined categories, and do not “inherit” or even “cause” the conflicts borne from the categories. Because the categories DO have conflicts, I agree; that’s just completely besides the point because I’m dealing with the actual things, not the categories
- Two: because both things do not cause each other, they are actually both a mutually arising manifestation of deeper patterns kf the universe (which I have been increasingly more and more aware of recently, but whose existence is so new and large and hard to match to any known category that I really have no better “name” for them besides “patterns of the universe”
- (Complete side note: [name] IS really good at dealing with the base things actually, but because she’s people focused, it manifests via working on the concepts and symbols people use. But this is not to say she works with the concepts - she uses the concepts to really quickly and blatantly show how conteadictory and arbitrary they are to shed light on the true nature of the things they are representing without ever “actually saying anything” about the things they represent. So cool)

- I have grown really fascinated by how the mind works when dreaming. It is such a crazy altered state of thinking that is so potent while it happens, but that leaves us so quickly. I have found very few pieces of art that comment on the nature of what it feels like to be in a dream rather than simply using a “dreamlike aesthetic”, which is sad, because I think the feeling of dreaming is so incredible and can make for such powerful and unique art. I also think that we can learn so much about how our minds work by examining what they do inside of dreams.
- Not to even MENTION lucid dreaming. Holy shit.
- For example, this is not a dream I had, but nevertheless shows “dream logic” well I think.
- I am hiding in a chest, and want to get out and go down a hallway to the left. However, there are many people in the room the chest resides in, and I want the room to be empty when I get out of the chest because I don’t want anybody to know that I got out. So I get out of the chest, tap the people on their shoulder and ask them to leave the room, then I go back inside the chest. The people leave, but more people enter the room. I get out of the chest again, and tell the new people that I want them to leave the room, since I want it to be empty to leave the chest. I return to the chest, they leave, but more people walk in. I get frustrated that people aren’t listening to me and the room isn’t clearing out, so I get out and go down the hallway to the right to try and devise some distraction to get the people away. Detail detail detail, some mini dream story happens in this area, and it ends with me “knowing” (but not seeing) that the room of people has emptied. As soon as this occurs, I run back to the room which is now still full of people and go down the left hallway. I find it leads to the same room as was down the right hallway, but I don’t find this weird at all and continue from there.
- Obviously a lot happened in that that isn’t realistic, but focus on the one big logical path that allowed many of the things to happen. I find that in dreams, your mind will latch on to a “flag” that will signify when an action is completed, and if somehow the action gets completed without the flag being triggered, your mind won’t actually register the action as being completed. And, if the flag somehow gets triggered, your brain will assume the action happened whether it actually did or not.
- For example, in the snippet above, my mind would have tied the flag of “the room is empty” to “me getting out of the chest and going down the left hallway”. As such, despite me repeatedly getting out of the chest and freely walking around, there are still people in the room, and so my brain is still stuck on “empty the room so you can leave the chest” and doesn’t register that I HAVE left the chest, so the room being empty doesn’t matter.
- Likewise, I know I didn’t fill in much detail for this part so it’s a little abstract, but consider when the room is empty. Sometimes in dreams you just “know something” without having been explicitly shown/told/etc, which is what this is - I just KNEW somehow that the room had emptied. As such, my mind suddenly goes “omg now you can get out of the chest and go down that left hallway” and I start on that action. When going back to the room, I find it still full of people, but that doesn’t matter - despite now being shown that the flag HADN’T actually triggered, my mind has nevertheless marked the flag as triggered, so I proceed as though the room was empty anyway.
- I also snuck in another thing of dream logic that results from this. When going down the left hallway, I ended up at the exact same room as when i went down the right hallway, but I didn’t find this strange or disheartening at all.
